name: pCloud
tagline: Sync and version selected folders against a user-owned object store

pricing.notes: Typical Premium Plus monthly price; lifetime plans also exist.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: Up to 10 GB storage after completing account-unlock steps.
tiers.notes: The account can start below 10 GB until the listed unlock actions are completed.

tiers.name: Premium 500 GB
tiers.limits: 500 GB storage; 500 GB shared-link traffic; 30-day file history.
tiers.notes: $49.99/year; a lifetime option is advertised at $199 one time (regular list $299).

tiers.name: Premium Plus 2 TB
tiers.limits: 2 TB storage; 2 TB shared-link traffic; 30-day file history.
tiers.notes: $99.99/year; a lifetime option is advertised at $399 one time (regular list $599).

tiers.name: Ultra 10 TB
tiers.limits: 10 TB storage; 2 TB shared-link traffic; 30-day file history.
tiers.notes: $299.99/year; a lifetime option is advertised at $1,190 one time (regular list $1,890).

pricing.freeTierCaps: up to 10 GB storage, unlocked through account actions
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual + separate lifetime one-time purchases; 14-day refund window
pricing.hiddenCosts: An extra 2 TB of shared-link traffic costs $9.99/month or $99.99/year. Links stop serving once traffic is exhausted until reset or an add-on is bought. Client-side pCloud Encryption is a separate paid add-on whose current price was not exposed.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For pCloud, sync and version selected folders against a user-owned object store. The hard boundary is cross-platform clients, media playback, sharing, optional encryption, and lifetime operations, plus reliability, durability, and cross-device sync.
coreLoopDIY: Sync selected folders against a user-owned object store, encrypt files client-side, track versions, and restore any version on demand.
whatYouLose: cross-platform clients, media playback, sharing, optional encryption, and lifetime operations
ongoingBurden: chunking, encryption, conflict detection, versions, garbage collection, bandwidth, restore drills, monitoring, billing, and disaster recovery
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for pCloud because storage subscriptions sell confidence that files will still exist after a lost device, bad sync, or provider incident. The recurring cost buys chunking, encryption, conflict detection, versions, garbage collection, bandwidth, restore drills, monitoring, billing, and disaster recovery, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Nextcloud
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source file sync and collaboration server.

alternatives.name: Nextcloud Files
alternatives.desc: Folder sync and versions over your own S3-compatible bucket; the metadata database becomes sacred.

alternatives.name: OpenCloud
alternatives.desc: A file cloud that can sit on S3-compatible storage, with sync clients and your name on every incident.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Seafile Community Edition
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Strong sync and versioning, but S3 storage is a Professional-edition feature, not the free server.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Premium Plus plan and a single-user encrypted backup DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for pCloud in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, MinIO, and a Tauri 2 sync client; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: sync selected folders against a user-owned object store, encrypt files client-side, track versions, and restore any version on demand.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Build a desktop client that watches explicitly selected folders and ignores configured patterns.
Chunk, hash, compress, and encrypt files locally before uploading to the configured object store.
Store version metadata, tombstones, device identifiers, and integrity checks in PostgreSQL.
Provide upload and restore queues with pause, retry, bandwidth limits, and resumable transfers.
Add file history, point-in-time restore, key export, storage usage, and scheduled restore tests.
Document the failure model and make clear that one server is not a complete backup strategy.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out multi-provider consumer sync at global scale.
Deliberately leave out guaranteed durability or ransomware recovery.
Deliberately leave out shared-drive administration, mobile apps, and enterprise compliance.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
